en: If Almambet remains here,
I will not remain alive without dying.
Concerning Almambet,
I hear bits and pieces of talk.
When his mother gave birth,
There were words that he would not live in peace;
Upon Kakancha, havoc—
That unbeliever has eyes that will bring it.
In his right hand, dark blood
He clutched as he fell, crying out;
He landed upright upon his feet.
Sounding the battle cry, “Ystan!”
In his left hand, black poison
He clutched as he fell, so I hear.
Dark blood in his right hand—
The reason he clutched it at birth
Was that in Beijing with its Kakancha,
Shedding blood and slaughtering people,
He meant to bring havoc.
Black poison in his left hand—
The reason he clutched it at birth
Was that until his dark head entered the dark earth,
The great men of Kakan Khan,
Gathered together
He meant to cut them down.
Cut down the willows of the valley;
They are going up in flames.
Aziz Khan's bastard fool,
My lord, restrain him now!
Either let me dwell in Beijing,
Or let him dwell in Beijing!”
Covering the ground beneath his feet,
Before Esen Khan
He had already spoken ill of him.
The unbelievers' khan, Khan Esen,
Flared up in anger;
That swine remained
Grumbling, unwilling to see him.
He turned Sarala's head.
“Alööke and Aziz are brothers;
He will judge the matter fairly.”
“Of the forty Chinese tribes, the people of Beijing,
Give me one khanship,” he said,
And stood requesting a khanship.
When he asked for the Shibe khanship,
“I gave it to Orokkyr,” he said,
And disappointed him there.
When he asked for the Manchu khanship,
“I gave it to Ezkara,” he said,
And disappointed him again.
When he asked for the Solon khanship,
“I gave it to Muzkindik,” he said,
Disappointing him in this way.
When he asked for the monks' khanship,
“I gave it to Konurbai,” he said,
And disappointed him there.
When he asked for the Torgut khanship,
“Kanyshai, with the armful-sized arse,
I gave it to that great woman,” he said,
And thus disappointed him.
Offended over the khanship,
He was left almost dead with grief.
And Esen Khan made him burn,
Reviling Almam;
He berated in this way
A wrestler like my Alake.
“Almambet, may you never reach maturity!
My child, may you never see next autumn!
This year your age has reached twelve.
Your head is not yet full of brains;
Wretch, your time to be khan has not yet come!
He was still somewhat childish and awkward,
If I give you the khanship of a place,
You will bring havoc.
The age for a khan is twenty-five;
Then you shall rule as khan.
Understand what you say!” he said,
And placed in his hand,
“Wear the stone of a shumbul official!”
Alake stood there in shame.
“Hey, dog, how can I accept what you say?
Among the forty Chinese tribes, the people of Beijing,
Not equal to a single khan,
How can I accept what you say?
I am the son of half a khan;
The stone of a shumbul, wretched soul,
How can I wear it without shame?
Not the equal of this Beijing,
How can I go on living without dying!”
Angry and ashamed,
In bitter distress:
“Esen Khan, who begrudges me a khanship,
If I do not seize him and take his head,
The golden throne beneath him,
If I do not seize it openly!”
Saying this, Alake
Turned Sarala's head.
To cut off Esen Khan's head,
To bring havoc,
He turned his horse's head,
And at Esen Khan's door
Kept watch for nine days.
Sarala was well fed;
For a fool like Esen Khan
The hour of death had not come.
Many sorrows filled his breast;
With a Chinese man like Esen Khan
God did not let him meet!
As he watched for nine days,
If Esen Khan came out the door,
You were going to kill me,
He intended to bring upon Beijing
Havoc that no one else could make.
The lion Almam meant to test
A swift horse like Sarala.
Alas, how well fed Sarala was!
Esen Khan, khan of Kakan—
The Chinese man's hour of death had not come.
As he watched Kakan,
Firmly harboring enmity toward Esen Khan,
He saw the loveliest of women;
At Esen Khan's doorway
He saw a girl who was a true Muslim.
He looked: Burulcha, Esen Khan's daughter,
Still a young child at play,
Her age not yet past twelve,
Her hair not yet long enough to braid.
Her waist like a sheath, her face like the moon,
The bold girl gazed serenely,
With thimble-small mouth and a young camel's eyes,
Her shining eyes glancing this way and that.
If snow falls upon the dark earth,
Look at the snow, then look at her skin.
If blood drips upon the snow,
Look at the blood, then look at her face.
(He looked: Burulcha, Esen's daughter.)
At that moment Alake said:
“Desiring the khanship of Beijing,
What wish shall I fulfill?
This Burulcha, Esen Khan's daughter,
Let me take her as my bride;
Let me cause a stir through this;
Let me seize the wretch's daughter.”
Saying this, Alake
Struck Sarala upon the flank.
Burulcha, Esen Khan's daughter,
He seized roughly by the neck,
Putting his hand upon her breast.
Then Burulcha spoke a word,
A harsh word that struck his breast:
“Take away your hand, Almambet!
Wretch, I will not listen to your answer.
Let me tell you something wonderful, Almam.”
Saying this, Burulcha continued:
“I tell you the truth, Almambet:
What is seen today is gone tomorrow;
Such is this shitty world!
Almambet, when I think of you,
My core burns, my heart is embers.
As his bride,
My Muslim people are not here.
Alake, you were a son of light;
I was a daughter of light.
Say ‘In God's name,’ come into the sunlight;
Alake, become a Muslim, enter the faith.
Scatter all that you have amassed,
Desire faith alone.
If you bring your tongue to the creed,
Almam, you might kill me without causing grief.
The road to the afterlife is near;
One who does not know the words is an unbeliever.
If you are free of the dark religion,
Almam, if you flee the unbelievers and become a stranger,
The road to Judgment is straitened;
Your faith is nearer than your far horizons.
Calling their bronze their God,
These Chinese people of yours are unbelievers.
Know this, Almam the leopard:
Say ‘In God's name’ and enter the faith.
Rather than become khan of the unbelievers,
Almam, may darkness take you, know this:
Would that you reached Mecca and settled there!
Rather than become khan of the Chinese,
Alake, would that you became a slave of the Kyrgyz!
The Prophet is true, your faith is true;
Renounced and abandoned,
Let the golden throne remain here.
The words I have spoken—
Will you heed them, Almambet?
That God is one,
Will you know it, Almambet?
Become a Muslim, enter the faith;
Alake, without turning aside, I will marry you.
I will turn my apple-like neck toward you.
‘This is my betrothed husband,’ I will say;
Alake, I will serve before you.
What is seen today is gone tomorrow;
Azazil somehow tricks us,
Such is this shitty world.
I have spoken precious words; understand them.
Alake, if fortune favors you, heed my words.
Bring your tongue to the creed;
If what I say is impious, kill me.
I shall see Muslim faces;
Almambet, come, let us go to the faith of Islam.
What shall we do by staying here?
My Alake, let us enter Mecca.
Where the ten stars in the sky
Set, let us go to that place.
Twelve ishans and forty sheikhs—
Alake, let us go where they rest!”
Good heavens, Burulcha spoke a word,
A harsh word that struck Almambet's heart.
Alake heard it in astonishment.
“What does ‘Muslim’ mean?
Who called this an unbeliever?
Everyone suffers torment;
What sort of talk does this furious girl utter?”
Nor was the courser Sarala at his side;
He had no thought then of becoming a Muslim.
Almam had not entered the Muslim faith;
He did not yet know the ways of belief.
She had drawn the line;
Burulcha, Esen Khan's daughter,
Had caused a stir for Almam.
“If you do not understand what I have said,
If you do not enter the Muslim faith,
Swelling with a struggle for khanship,
You have come to the city of Beijing.
One like you, who does not sit to urinate,
Whose hem does not touch the ground,
Of God Most High, the One,
Who does not know His unity,
Of the bare ground where horses are tied,
Of a babbling unbeliever like you,
Now remain out in the wilderness!
Of a faithless unbeliever like you—
Not my breast, remember,
Two thousand of you gathered together
Are worth less than the hem of my dress!
I will not listen to your talk.
Take away your hand, Chinese man.
I tell you to become a Muslim, but you refuse,
Reaching out your great hands as before,
You will not abandon your Chinese ways!”
Then, raging, she flung it aside,
Tore away my hand,
Throwing it a spear's length from her breast.
“The faith I desire is Islam;
The husband I seek is a Muslim.
Upon a babbling Kalmyk,
Far from marrying him, I would not even piss.
If my precious life is spared,
I will not remain among Beijing's people.”
Then Alake stood and thought:
“What does ‘Chinese’ mean?
